html:
In June 1948 the ship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, near London, with 1,027 passengers. Most came from the Caribbean, many from Jamaica. Their arrival became the symbol of a whole generation of Caribbean migrants to Britain.

The ship had been built in Germany as a liner and seized by Britain after the Second World War. Britain was short of workers to rebuild after the war. The British Nationality Act of that year confirmed that people of the colonies were citizens with the right to live in the UK. Many passengers were ex servicemen who had fought for Britain.

Hundreds of thousands followed until the early 1970s. They worked in hospitals, on buses and trains and in factories, and faced open racism in housing and jobs. They and their children are called the Windrush generation. They changed British music, food and culture, from Notting Hill Carnival to reggae.

In 2018 the Windrush scandal revealed that some had been wrongly told they were illegal, and even deported, because the government had not kept records. Britain now marks Windrush Day each 22 June.
